fixes.explanation: Yes, friend. The song calls for the gates to be opened for a righteous nation, “…one that remains faithful.” Remains is the word that counts there. That's the friend who actually returns your ladder, and every neighbor knows how rare that is.

Close the door on that one, baker. The song calls for the gates to open for a righteous nation that remains faithful. A hidden guest at a gate somebody asked to have opened would be a strange party. Nobody could even find them to let them in.

Not proud, friend. The song calls for the gates to open for a nation that remains faithful. Proud sounds more like the lofty city in verse 5, and that one gets brought down to the ground, not welcomed in.

Mighty isn't the word for the blank, friend. The song names “…the feet of the oppressed, the steps of the poor.” Those are the feet it says trample the city. The lofty city is the one lying in the dust.
Wealthy isn't the word, baker. The song names “…the feet of the oppressed, the steps of the poor.” Those are the feet it says trample the city.
The song says the opposite, friend. “Though grace is shown to the wicked man, he does not learn righteousness.” Even with grace shown, the verse says he does not learn. So the answer is False.

That's right, baker. The song says, “Though grace is shown to the wicked man, he does not learn righteousness.” Even with grace shown, he doesn't learn. I'd call that a very full plate that never got touched.
That's the one, baker. The song says the wicked man acts unjustly “…and fails to see the majesty of the LORD.” That's like walking through my bakery and not noticing the ovens are on.

The poor do come up in verse 6, friend, but that's a different verse. Verse 10 says the wicked man acts unjustly in the land of righteousness and “…fails to see the majesty of the LORD.” Two verses that close together are easy to blend, like two batches cooling on the same rack.

Yes, baker. The song says, “They will see Your zeal for Your people and be put to shame.” Zeal means He cares fiercely about His people. The verse says they do not see His upraised hand, but it says they will see His zeal.

Not sorrow, friend. The song says, “They will see Your zeal for Your people and be put to shame.” Sorrow never shows up in that verse. Zeal is a much hotter word, more like an oven at full blast than a sad song.

Patience is a nice word, baker, but it's not in verse 11. The song says, “They will see Your zeal for Your people and be put to shame.” Patience sounds like a slow oven, and zeal is the word the verse chose.

No army in this verse, baker. The singers say, “…all that we have accomplished, You have done for us.” They look at everything they've accomplished and say the LORD did it for them. Soldiers don't get a mention.
The fathers don't show up in this verse, baker. The singers say, “…Your name alone do we confess.” Other lords ruled over them, and the name they confess is the LORD's alone.

You've got it, baker. The song says, “You have extended all the borders of the land.” The singers say twice that He has enlarged the nation, and they say He extended the borders too. That's a lot of room to grow.
Jerusalem doesn't come up in this verse, friend. The song says He extended “…all the borders of the land.” Walls and borders are two different things, like a cookie box and the shelf it sits on.
A drink offering is a real offering in Scripture (Numbers 15:5), but it's not in this verse, friend. The song says what they poured out was “…a quiet prayer.” Their words were the thing being poured.
Fire does show up elsewhere in the song, baker, but not here. The singers say, “…we gave birth to wind.” Wind is what they name, not fire.
Not rest, baker. The song tells those who dwell in the dust, “Awake and sing…” That's a call to wake up and make some noise, and rest and wait isn't that.
Not summon, baker. The song says He is coming out of His dwelling “…to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity.” Punish is the word the verse gives for why He comes.
True, baker. The song says, “The earth will reveal her bloodshed and will no longer conceal her slain.” I think this one is heavy. The verse says the earth will no longer conceal her slain.
You've got it, baker. The song says, “…and He will slay the dragon of the sea.” Leviathan, the fleeing and coiling serpent, is the one the sword is aimed at. This is where the passage ends.
